notes:
I found plenty of verse-by-verse commentary on Isaiah 51. The gaps are elsewhere. I found no Catholic or Orthodox pages, no prosperity, Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, and no source that sets out clear denominational disagreement. Where commentators do differ, I name the commentator rather than give him a tradition label the page doesn't give.

## Overview
- Constable divides vv. 1–8 into three calls to "listen": look back to what God did (1–3), look up to who God is (4–6), and don't be afraid, remembering what God promised (7–8). He also sees the whole chapter building toward the Servant Song of 52:13–53:12. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- Bridgeway sets the scene: to the Jews in Babylon, getting free and rebuilding seemed impossible. God encourages them by reminding them of the apparently impossible things he has done for them in the past. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/isaiah-51.html

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- **Who is addressed:** the faithful exiles who don't "seek after idols," as many others did. "Look to the rock" means look back at Israel's small beginnings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **What the rock stands for (commentators disagree):**
  - Gill says Abraham is called a rock not so much for the strength of his faith, as for his old age; when he looked like a hard dry rock, from whom no issue could be expected. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/51-1.htm
  - Calvin rejects both the "strong faith" and the "old age" readings. For him it is a simple metaphor, taken from quarries, meaning only that they descend from Abraham and Sarah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-51.html
  - Matthew Henry reads the verse as a call to humility: remember the hard rock and miserable pit you came from, so think little of yourself and much of grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_051.cfm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) disagrees. The point is not, as it is often quoted, the inculcation of humility, but that the God who called and blessed Abraham can restore them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/51-1.htm
  - Gill reports that Jerome, and Cocceius after him, took the rock to be Christ, with the church coming from his pierced side. (This is Gill's report; I didn't find Jerome himself.) Same URL.
- **What "pursue righteousness" means (also disputed):**
  - Benson: seeking justification, sanctification and obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-51.html
  - Cambridge Bible: right conduct, not "salvation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/51-1.htm
  - JFB: Israel's mistake was pursuing righteousness "by the works of the law," instead of 'by faith,' as Abraham did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-51.html

**v. 2**
- **God's call of one man:** "When he was but one" means before he had children. If God could multiply one man, he could much more rebuild a nation from the remnant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Spurgeon:** the lesson is the Lord working the greatest results from apparently inadequate causes. Abraham's defining trait was faith, but the main thought must be God himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/51-2.html
- **Guzik:** God doesn't need many people. The exiles, and Israel's final regathering, shouldn't be discouraged by small numbers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/

**v. 3**
- **Grammar:** the Hebrew literally says "has comforted," because God has settled the matter. Judea had become literal wilderness during the exile, and the prophet compares its restoration to Eden (as Ezekiel does). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable, quoting Motyer and Delitzsch:**
  - Motyer: Eden also means the curse is gone.
  - Delitzsch: Zion is a "second Sarah," surrounded by children after long barrenness.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Guzik:** the near fulfilment was the return from Babylon. The ultimate one is a restored Israel in the millennium. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/

**v. 4**
- **Pulpit:** "the law" is probably the Christian "law," the new covenant, which the apostles' preaching made a light to the peoples. It also notes that the variant reading "O ye nations" is wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable:** "law" is torah, meaning instruction. God's faithfulness to Israel becomes a lesson to the world, as the Servant was to bring justice to the nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 5**
- **Pulpit:**
  - Isaiah always writes as if the Messiah's kingdom follows straight after the return. He wasn't shown the 500–600-year gap.
  - The "arm" is God's power to carry out his purposes.
  - Gentiles received Christianity more readily than Israel did.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable:** Cyrus brought deliverance to the Israelites from Babylon, but the Servant would bring salvation to the nations of the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 6**
- **Pulpit:** even what seems most permanent will pass away, but God's salvation will not. Dr Kay notes that people don't simply vanish the way things do, because humans keep existing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Guzik:** the passing away of heaven and earth belongs to events around the Second Coming. God won't change his character or his mind about us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/
- **JFB (word study):** "vanish" may mean "torn apart like a garment." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-51.html

**v. 7**
- **Pulpit:** this addresses the highest grade of faithfulness: people who have found God, not just those still seeking (v. 1). They can still be tempted to fear what others think. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Guzik:** cites Spurgeon on the cowardice of being ashamed of Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/

**v. 8**
- **Pulpit:** people may continue to exist, but their verdicts and opinions perish completely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable:** the critics fade away, while those who trust God last. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 9**
- **Who is speaking:** suggestions include Zion, the prophet, angels, God, and the Son pleading with the Father. Pulpit thinks the prophet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **"Awake":** God doesn't actually sleep. Guzik says it is the faithful believer calls out to the LORD, looking to Him for salvation. He adds that it wakes up *our* faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/
- **A sermon on the reply:** the Biblical Illustrator material pairs this verse with 52:1, where God answers "Awake, O Zion." The point: it isn't God who is asleep. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/51-9.htm
- **What Rahab and the dragon mean (readings differ):**
  - Pulpit: Rahab ("pride") is Egypt, destroyed at the Red Sea. The "dragon" is Pharaoh (Ezek 29:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
  - Guzik: it describes, in poetry, God's victory over Satan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/
  - NET Bible notes (modern scholarship): a symbolic sea monster, known elsewhere in the Bible and in Ugaritic myth as Leviathan. This sea creature symbolizes the forces of chaos that seek to destroy the created order. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Isa+51%3A9-10
  - Constable combines these: it means Egypt, but the prophet borrows ancient myth to show the LORD defeats every pagan god. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 10**
- **Pulpit:** this is the single Red Sea crossing. That sea is called "the great deep" because it connects to the ocean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable:** pagans told of gods drying up a chaos-sea at creation. Isaiah points to an actual historical event instead. He wonders whether Isaiah's "way" imagery lies behind early Christians calling their faith "the Way." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 11**
- **Pulpit:** this nearly repeats 35:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Coffman:** the return from Babylon is treated as "a new exodus." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Constable:** the return was a foretaste of the joy of the millennium. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 12**
- **Barnes:** the repeated "I" stresses that comfort comes from God alone. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-51.html
- **Does God answer the prayer of v. 9?** Pulpit says this passage is "certainly not an answer" to vv. 9–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm Constable says vv. 12–16 *are* the Lord's response. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 13**
- **Pulpit:** the charge isn't apostasy but lack of a living, practical faith. The oppressor's rage ends when Persia conquers Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable, quoting Oswalt:** living in fear of people amounts to forgetting God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 14**
- **Pulpit:** the phrase means "he who is bent down" by fetters will soon be released. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Constable:** read it collectively: the nation won't die out in exile. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Henry:** God can rescue people however low they've been brought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_051.cfm

**v. 15**
- **Translation note:** KJV/Pulpit read "divided the sea," another reference to the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm JFB favours Gesenius's sense, close to BSB's "stirs up." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-51.html

**v. 16**
- **Henry:** the prophets' and apostles' words were God's own words. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_051.cfm
- **Servant language:**
  - Cambridge Bible: Servant language is here applied to Israel, which supports the view that the Servant personifies Israel.
  - Some scholars (Cheyne) think the verse is a fragment that slipped in from another context.
  - Ellicott: this is the first hint of the new heavens and new earth.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/51-16.htm
- **Constable:** only the ideal Israel, the Servant, fully fulfils it. He also reports Watts's unusual view that the speaker is Darius. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Guzik:** "the shadow of my hand" recalls God covering Moses in the rock (Exod 33). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/

**v. 17**
- **Benson:** a call to wake not so much out of the sleep of sin though that also was necessary, in order to their being ready for deliverance, as out of the stupor of despondency and despair. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-51.html
- **Guzik:** the cup is a common Old Testament picture of judgment, here the Babylonian conquest, and Jesus had this cup in mind in Gethsemane. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-51/

**vv. 18–20**
- **Constable:** neither mother nor children can help. Because she deserved her punishment, she couldn't be comforted like an innocent victim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Pulpit:** read "gazelle in a net," exhausted from famine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/51.htm
- **Lowth (via Benson):** nowhere is the cup image handled with more force. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 21**
- **Constable:** "Therefore" moves from danger to promise. Oswalt contrasts self-sufficient Babylon with Zion, who knows she is afflicted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html

**v. 22**
- **Constable:** God will not punish them this way again because the Servant will drink the cup for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Christ drinking the cup:** teachers in several traditions agree here rather than differ.
  - **Reformed (Sproul, Ligonier):** Christ drank the cup for all who put their trust in Him. https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/the-cup-of-gods-wrath
  - **Gospel Coalition article (Andrew Hebert):** Jesus shrank back knowing he'd be absorbing the fury of God—which was rightfully ours—in our place. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-good-news-of-the-empty-cup/
  - **Desiring God:** links the goblet of Isa 51:17 to Gethsemane. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/agony-in-the-garden
  - **Lutheran (1517):** adds a link to the Lord's Supper. Because Jesus drained the wrath, believers can tip the cup to our lips and drink eternal life. https://www.1517.org/articles/jesus-drains-the-cup-so-we-may-drink

**v. 23**
- **Constable:** walking on captives' backs is about humiliating them, not killing them (Josh 10:24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-51.html
- **Bridgeway:** the cup passes to Babylon, which will fall as Judah did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/isaiah-51.html

## Where readings divide
**When it will be fulfilled:**
- Guzik and Constable see a near fulfilment (the return from Babylon) and a final one in a future millennium (vv. 3, 11, 16).
- Pulpit applies vv. 4–5 to the Christian new covenant and the Gentile mission.
- Neither page ties its reading to a denomination.

## Not found
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found nothing on Isaiah 51 from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. Jerome's view comes only secondhand through Gill (v. 1).
- **Prosperity, Word of Faith, hyper-grace:** I found no material on this chapter.
